summaries.example: Imagine an apple. You can see its color and shape, feel its skin, smell it, and taste it. Berkeley says the apple is the group of these experiences together. If you close your eyes, the apple can still be there to experience later because the world follows steady rules.
summaries.summary: George Berkeley defended a surprising view called idealism. He rejected mind-independent matter, but he did not deny everyday objects such as trees, books, or apples. Instead, he said an object is a collection of ideas—things experienced through sight, touch, taste, smell, or hearing. Minds are different from ideas because minds perceive and act. Berkeley thought our changing sense experiences are caused by another spirit, God, and that nature stays dependable because God follows regular laws. He also argued that science is useful because it discovers these regular patterns, even if it does not uncover material causes.
key_ideas: Berkeley argued against the idea that material things exist outside all minds.
He said ordinary objects are groups of ideas that regularly appear together.
His famous claim means that things, except perceiving minds, exist by being perceived.
He believed God causes our sense experiences and keeps nature orderly.
summaries.why_it_matters: Berkeley asks us to examine what it means for something to be real. His view connects everyday experiences with large questions about minds, the world, God, and science. Even if we disagree with him, his arguments help us notice the difference between what we experience and what we think exists beyond experience.

important_terms.definition: The view that reality is made only of minds and the ideas they perceive.
A mind-independent thing: something that would exist even if no mind perceived it.
Something a mind notices, such as a color, sound, taste, or shape.
A thinking and perceiving being, such as a person or, for Berkeley, God.

questions_to_think_about: When you leave a room, what do you mean when you say the chair is still there?
Could two people experience the same apple in exactly the same way?
Why might steady patterns in nature matter to Berkeley?

summaries.example: Suppose a desk is in a locked office. A representationalist materialist might say that you directly experience an idea of the desk, which represents a mind-independent desk outside you. Berkeley challenges this picture in two ways: he questions whether an idea can resemble something unlike an idea, and he argues that matter does not explain how a physical body produces an experience in a mind. He instead treats the desk as a lawful collection of ideas, whose continued availability depends on God's ordering of experience.
summaries.summary: George Berkeley's philosophy attacks materialism and develops an idealist alternative. In the target view, ordinary objects are mind-independent substances, while perception is representational: we immediately perceive ideas and infer external objects that those ideas represent. Berkeley argues that this inference fails because an idea cannot resemble a fundamentally non-mental substance, and because abstract notions such as bare extension cannot be formed in the way his opponents require. He also claims that matter does not explain the production of ideas, since the interaction of body and mind remains unexplained. Berkeley's alternative is not that nothing exists, but that reality includes passive ideas and active spirits. Objects such as apples and trees are ordered collections of ideas. God, an infinite spirit, causes sensory ideas and supplies the regularity that makes a shared, predictable physical world possible. On this framework, scientific laws describe dependable patterns in experience rather than material mechanisms operating independently of minds. The entry also notes unresolved pressures concerning unperceived objects, error, shared objects, and the causal powers of spirits.
key_ideas: Berkeley's central target is materialism understood as the doctrine that material things exist, especially mind-independent substances.
His core argument begins from the idea-theoretic premise that what is immediately perceived is an idea, then challenges attempts to infer material objects behind ideas.
The likeness principle and anti-abstractionism attack proposed ways of characterizing matter as something resembling sensory ideas or as bare extension.
Berkeley argues that matter is not needed to explain ideas: materialists still face the difficulty of explaining how an extended body affects a non-extended mind.
His positive ontology contains passive ideas, active spirits, and God, who causes the systematic sensory ideas of finite minds.
Science remains useful because it identifies lawful connections among phenomena and supports prediction, even though Berkeley denies that bodies are the ultimate causes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Berkeley's arguments force a careful separation between perception, representation, and reality. They also show how a theory can preserve ordinary objects and scientific prediction while rejecting matter as traditionally understood. His philosophy remains important because it tests whether explanations based on mind-independent substances are actually clearer than the experiences they are meant to explain, while raising difficult questions about divine agency, object permanence, and causal power.

important_terms.definition: Berkeley's view that reality consists exclusively of minds and their ideas; ordinary objects are mind-dependent collections of ideas.
The claim that a material object exists independently of any perceiving or thinking mind.
A theory saying that we directly perceive ideas, which stand for or represent external material objects.
Berkeley's claim that an idea can resemble only another idea, not a non-mental material substance.
Berkeley's rejection of the view that the mind can form intrinsically general ideas by removing particular features from a particular idea.
An active perceiver or thinker, contrasted with passive ideas; Berkeley uses this term for finite minds and God.
The doctrine that to exist, a sensible thing is to be perceived, while a mind exists by perceiving or acting.
Berkeley's account of science as discovering stable patterns and rules in experience rather than material efficient causes.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that a representation is in the mind show that what it represents must also be mind-dependent?
Can sensory relativity show that qualities such as heat or color are not properties of mind-independent objects?
Is a regular pattern in experience an adequate substitute for a material cause?
Does God's role solve the problem of objects continuing to exist when no finite person perceives them?
What is the difference between having a mistaken perception and making a mistaken judgment from a perception?

summaries.example: Think about a mug of hot chocolate. One person may call it hot, while another person with cold hands may experience it differently. Berkeley uses cases like this to question whether sensory qualities belong to objects exactly as we experience them. He would say that what we directly encounter is an idea, and that a mug is a dependable collection of ideas—its looks, feel, smell, and taste. Its dependable return when we come back is explained by regular patterns in nature, ultimately connected with God.
summaries.summary: George Berkeley defended idealism, a theory that reality contains minds and ideas rather than mind-independent material substances. He did not say that trees, houses, or books are imaginary. He said they are collections of ideas that appear together in stable ways: an apple, for example, includes visual, tactile, tasty, and fragrant experiences. Berkeley criticized representationalism, the idea that our ideas copy or represent material objects behind experience. He argued that an idea cannot resemble a completely different kind of thing, and that matter does not really explain how ideas are produced in minds. Berkeley's own view includes passive ideas and active spirits. Human minds can imagine some ideas, but sense experiences arrive without our choosing them. Berkeley therefore argued that another spirit, God, causes the ordered experiences of nature. Science remains valuable because it finds regular connections and helps us predict what will happen.
key_ideas: Berkeley challenged materialism, meaning the belief that material things exist independently of minds.
He argued that we experience ideas directly, so sensory qualities cannot simply be assumed to belong to external matter.
He questioned whether matter explains our experiences, since it is unclear how a physical body could produce an idea in a mind.
He still accepted everyday objects, describing them as groups of ideas that regularly occur together.
God is central to Berkeley's explanation of why sensory experiences are orderly and do not depend only on our choices.
Berkeley thought science discovers patterns in experience that help us explain and predict events.
summaries.why_it_matters: Berkeley's philosophy makes us ask whether we know the world directly or only through experiences in our minds. It also challenges the assumption that adding invisible matter automatically gives a better explanation. His view connects questions about perception with questions about reality, science, and God's role in nature.

important_terms.definition: The view that reality is made up of minds and the ideas those minds experience, rather than mind-independent matter.
A thing that would exist even if no mind were thinking about or experiencing it.
Something experienced by a mind, such as a color, sound, texture, smell, or taste.
The view that we experience ideas directly and that these ideas represent objects outside the mind.
The claim that an idea can be similar only to another idea, not to a non-thinking material object.
A perceiving and acting mind. Berkeley calls human minds and God spirits.

questions_to_think_about: If two people experience the same object differently, does that show the object has no mind-independent qualities?
Is an object still real if nobody is looking at it?
Why might Berkeley think that matter fails to explain how sensations happen?
Can a theory reject matter while still preserving ordinary objects and useful science?
